explanations.explanation: Mourning is the word. The LORD says, “…there will be mourning and lamentation…” Two heavy words stacked right next to each other. I think this part of the passage hurts, friend.

I see why you went there. The verse before this one says, “Year upon year let your festivals recur.” But verse 2 turns the corner, and the LORD says there will be “…mourning and lamentation…” The mood changes fast, and I think this is a heavy turn.

Trading sounds busy and practical, but the verse doesn't mention it. The LORD says that after He constrains Ariel, “…there will be mourning and lamentation…” Those are the words to hold onto. Easy mix-up when you're thinking about a city, though.

That's it. The LORD says, “I will besiege you with towers and set up siege works against you.” Notice who's doing the camping. David, Israel's king, once camped at Ariel, and now the LORD says, “I will camp in a circle around you…”

Chariots and horsemen sound like a natural fit for a battle, I get it. But this verse never mentions them. It says the LORD will besiege Ariel “…with towers and set up siege works against you.” Stick with what the text hands you and you can't go far off.

Spears and shields are the classic battle gear, so that guess makes sense. The verse doesn't list them, though. It says the LORD will set up “towers” and “siege works.” Those are built to surround a city, and the verse says He camps in a circle around her.

Dust is right. The verse says, “You will be brought low, you will speak from the ground, and out of the dust your words will be muffled.” That's a city talking from as low as it gets. Picture someone mumbling into the floor, and you're close.

Rooftops would be the opposite direction, friend. A voice from a rooftop carries far. This verse goes the other way: “You will be brought low…” and the words come “…out of the dust…” Low and muffled is the whole picture.

City gates are a fair guess, since a city has plenty of them. But the verse never says gates. It says her words will be muffled “…out of the dust…” and her speech “…will whisper out of the dust.” The ground is where this voice comes from.

I'm glad you took a swing, but this one runs the other way. Verse 5 says “…suddenly, in an instant…” and then verse 6 says Ariel “…will be visited by the LORD of Hosts…” Nothing slow or little-by-little about it. It's an instant, like when the oven timer goes off and you swear you only blinked.
False is right. Verse 5 says “Then suddenly, in an instant…” and verse 6 says Ariel “…will be visited by the LORD of Hosts…” No slow trickle here. It all arrives at once.

True. Isaiah 29:6 says Ariel will be visited by the LORD of Hosts “…with thunder and earthquake and loud noise…” The text lines up the sounds and the shaking right along with the visit. You'd know it the second it arrived.

I think the word visit sounded gentle, like a friendly stop-by. But the verse says Ariel “…will be visited by the LORD of Hosts with thunder and earthquake and loud noise…” So the visit comes with thunder and earthquake right alongside. This is no quiet knock on the door.
Yes, still hungry. The verse says he dreams he is eating, “…then awakens still hungry…” That's the picture for the nations that attack Ariel.
That would be a nice dream, wouldn't it? But the verse says the opposite. He dreams he is eating, “…then awakens still hungry…” The dream feast doesn't carry over into real life.

Forgetting the dream isn't in the text. The verse says he dreams he is eating, “…then awakens still hungry…” So the hunger is what he wakes up with. The picture is about the empty feeling, not a lost memory.

Mount Zion it is. The verse says, “So will it be for all the many nations who go to battle against Mount Zion.” The dreamers wake up still hungry and still thirsty, and that's the picture for those nations.
Ooh, Sinai! Big name. Famous mountains love to crash a verse they weren't invited to. This one doesn't name it, though. The nations “…go to battle against Mount Zion.”
Carmel, huh? Wrong mountain for this verse, friend, and it's out of its lane here. The text says the many nations “…go to battle against Mount Zion.” Zion is the one on this map.

I get why you'd think so, with all that staggering. But the verse says the opposite: “be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not from strong drink.” So the wobble comes from somewhere else. The text says no to wine and no to strong drink.

False is right. The verse says, “be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not from strong drink.” The staggering is real, but wine and strong drink aren't the cause. The next verse points to what the LORD has done.
Yes. Verse 10 says, “For the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.” Poured out, like it's filling a cup. That would explain the stumbling in the last verse.

Smoke would sure make it hard to see, so that guess has a reason behind it. But the verse says, “…the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.” No smoke is mentioned. It's sleep that gets poured out.
Pouring does sound like rain, I'll give you that. But the thing poured out here is “…a spirit of deep sleep.” The verse doesn't mention rain or a flood. It's about sleep, and it's heavy.

That's right. The verse says, “He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers.” These are the very people you'd expect to see clearly. Instead their eyes are shut and their heads are covered.

Kings and princes are big names in a city, so I see the guess. But the verse speaks to someone else: “He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers.” Kings aren't mentioned here. It's the prophets and the seers.
Farmers and shepherds work hard, but they aren't named in this verse. It says, “He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers.” The ones named are the prophets and the seers.
True. The verse says that if the scroll is handed to someone to read, “he will say, ‘I cannot, because it is sealed.’” The words are right there, locked up inside. He can't get to them.

This one is easy to doubt, but the verse says it plainly. If the scroll is handed to someone to read, “he will say, ‘I cannot, because it is sealed.’” The seal is what stops him. A sealed scroll stays shut until somebody opens it.

Yes, unable. Verse 12 says, “Or if the scroll is handed to one unable to read…” and then he says he cannot read. So the scroll is closed to the first person because it's sealed, and to this one because he can't read it. Either way, the words stay out of reach.
Fear is a believable reason, but the text doesn't give one. It says the scroll is handed to “…one unable to read…” and he says he cannot read. The word here is unable.
Eager would make a nice story, but that's not what the verse says. It's “…one unable to read…” and his answer is “I cannot read.” Wanting to read it doesn't change the picture. He can't.
That's right. The Lord says, “…but their hearts are far from Me.” The mouths are close and the hearts are far. He looks at both.

That would be a happy ending, but the Lord says the reverse. These people draw near with their mouths and honor Him with their lips, “…but their hearts are far from Me.” The word “but” is the turning point. Their hearts aren't close at all.
Loyal sounds like it fits all that lip honor. The Lord says otherwise, though: “…but their hearts are far from Me.” The lips honor Him, and the hearts are far from Him. Far is the word.
Yes. The Lord says, “Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men.” He says it right after saying their hearts are far from Him. The people's worship of Him is called rules taught by men.
Songs fit with worship, so I see the pull. But the Lord doesn't say songs. He says, “Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men.” Those are rules, and the people are the ones who taught them.
Far away is a good clue, since the hearts are far from the Lord. But He doesn't call their worship a gift. He says, “Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men.” The word to hold is rules.
That's the one. The Lord says, “Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder.” Wonder stacked on wonder, one right after another. It's a lot to take in.

Storms do show up earlier in this passage, in verse 6, so I see why that stuck in your head. But verse 14 has the Lord saying He will confound these people “…with wonder upon wonder.” Wonder is the word here, not storm.
Silence upon silence has a nice ring to it. But the Lord says, “…I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder.” He doesn't say silence. It's wonder, stacked up high.
I can see why growing wisdom sounds like the good-news version. But the Lord says the reverse: “The wisdom of the wise will vanish…” Vanish is the opposite of grow. It's gone.
False is right. The Lord says, “The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.” No growing in sight. It goes away and gets hidden.
